WASHINGTON (CNN) -- The government is warning that taking the psoriasis drug Raptiva could result in serious brain infection and even death. Raptiva may cause a serious brain infection called progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. The Food and Drug Administration cited three confirmed cases, and a possible fourth, of people diagnosed with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) after being treated with Raptiva. "Three of those patients have died," the FDA said in a public health advisory. "All four patients were treated with the drug for more than three years." None was receiving other treatments that suppress the immune system. Raptiva's product labeling was revised in October to highlight a boxed warning about the risks of life-threatening infections, including PML. "At that time, the FDA directed Genentech, the manufacturer, to develop a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS) to include a medication guide to educate patients about the drug's risks," the FDA's advisory says. In the advisory, issued Thursday, the FDA highlighted the confirmed cases and promised to "take appropriate steps" to ensure that Raptiva's risks do not outweigh its benefits. The FDA also said it will ensure that patients "are clearly informed of the signs and symptoms of PML" and that health care professionals "carefully monitor patients for the possible development of PML." Overseas, the European Medicines Agency has gone further, recommending that no new prescriptions for Raptiva be issued and that patients taking the drug talk to their doctors about an alternative. On Thursday it asked the European Commission to make that recommendation legally binding. The group's Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use determined "that the benefits of Raptiva no longer outweigh its risks, because of safety concerns, including the occurrence of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in patients taking the medicine." It said patients who have been treated with the drug should be "closely monitored for neurological symptoms and symptoms of infection." "Patients who are currently taking Raptiva should not stop treatment abruptly, but should make an appointment with their doctor to discuss the most appropriate replacement treatment," the agency said. Raptiva, a once-weekly injection for adults with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis, works by suppressing T-cells -- cells that help fight infection -- in the immune system. Those cells cause the skin inflammation associated with psoriasis. By suppressing T-cells, Raptiva "decreases the function of the immune system, which increases a patient's susceptibility to infections," the FDA said. The National Institutes of Health says the prognosis for PML "remains grim; the disease usually lasts for months and 80 percent die within the first six months, although spontaneous improvement has been reported. Those who survive PML can be left with severe neurological disabilities." Around 6 million to 7 million Americans have psoriasis, which is incurable, the NIH says.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has issued a public health advisory warning healthcare providers and patients that Raptiva, a prescription medication used to treat moderate to severe plaque psoriasis, may increase the risk of developing a rare but serious brain infection known as progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). The drug, manufactured by the biotechnology company Genentech, has been linked to this potentially fatal condition primarily among patients who have used the medication over an extended period.

According to the FDA's advisory, the agency identified three confirmed cases of PML, along with a possible fourth case, all occurring in long-term users of the drug. The infection is caused by a virus that typically affects individuals whose immune systems have been compromised. Because Raptiva works by suppressing certain components of the immune system to reduce the inflammation associated with psoriasis, it may leave patients more vulnerable to this type of opportunistic infection.

The severity of the situation was underscored by the fact that three of the four affected patients ultimately died as a result of the infection. # FDA Warns of Fatal Brain Infection Risk Linked to Psoriasis Drug Raptiva

**Health authorities advise patients to consult physicians as safety concerns mount over immune-suppressing medication**

---

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has issued a public health advisory warning that Raptiva (efalizumab), a prescription medication used to treat moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, has been associated with a rare but often fatal brain infection.

## The Safety Warning

The FDA advisory highlights reports of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) among patients taking Raptiva, including several confirmed deaths. PML is a serious and typically fatal viral disease that attacks the central nervous system, damaging the white matter of the brain. There is currently no known effective treatment or cure for the condition.

The infection has been reported primarily in patients who received the drug for an extended period, generally more than three years of continuous use.

## How Raptiva Works

Raptiva belongs to a class of drugs known as immunosuppressants. The medication works by suppressing certain immune cells, called T-cells, that contribute to the inflammation and rapid skin cell growth characteristic of psoriasis.

While this immune-suppressing action helps control psoriasis symptoms, it also weakens the body's overall defenses. This reduced immune activity is believed to allow the JC virus—a common virus that lies dormant and harmless in most healthy people—to become active and attack the brain, leading to PML.

## What Patients Should Do

Health officials are urging patients and healthcare providers to take the following precautions:

- **Do not stop the medication abruptly.** Patients currently taking Raptiva should not discontinue the drug on their own but should contact their doctor to discuss the risks and benefits.

- **Consult your physician.** Patients should talk with their healthcare provider about whether continued treatment is appropriate and explore alternative therapies for managing psoriasis.

- **Watch for warning signs.** Patients should seek immediate medical attention if they experience symptoms that may indicate PML, including:
  - Progressive weakness on one side of the body
  - Clumsiness or difficulty with coordination
  - Vision changes or disturbances
  - Confusion, memory problems, or personality changes
  - Difficulty speaking

- **Report new neurological symptoms** to a doctor without delay.

## The Bigger Picture

The advisory reflects the delicate balance regulators and physicians must strike when weighing the benefits of immune-modulating drugs against their potential risks. For patients with severe psoriasis whose quality of life is significantly affected, treatment decisions require careful, individualized medical guidance.

The FDA has stated it will continue to monitor safety data and update its recommendations as needed. Patients with concerns are encouraged to speak directly with their healthcare providers.

---

# FDA and EMA Warnings on Raptiva (Efalizumab): A Cautionary Chapter in Psoriasis Treatment

## Introduction

In 2009, regulatory authorities on both sides of the Atlantic took decisive action against Raptiva (efalizumab), a biologic medication once heralded as a breakthrough treatment for chronic plaque psoriasis. Following reports of a rare but frequently fatal brain infection, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) issued serious warnings that ultimately led to the drug's withdrawal from the market. This case remains an important lesson in pharmacovigilance and the ongoing balance between therapeutic benefit and patient risk.

## Understanding Psoriasis: The Underlying Condition

Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory disease that primarily affects the skin. It occurs when the immune system mistakenly accelerates the skin cell life cycle, causing cells to build up rapidly on the skin's surface. This results in the characteristic symptoms of the disease:

- **Raised, red patches** covered with silvery-white scales (plaques)
- **Itching, burning, or soreness** in affected areas
- **Dry, cracked skin** that may bleed
- **Thickened or ridged nails**
- **Stiff and swollen joints** in cases involving psoriatic arthritis

Plaque psoriasis is the most common form, accounting for roughly 80–90% of cases. The condition affects approximately 2–3% of the global population and is associated with significant physical discomfort and psychological burden, including depression and reduced quality of life. Beyond skin symptoms, psoriasis is linked to comorbidities such as cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, and psoriatic arthritis.

While there is no cure, treatments aim to reduce inflammation, slow skin cell turnover, and manage symptoms. Therapies range from topical treatments and phototherapy to systemic medications and biologics—the latter category to which Raptiva belonged.

## What Was Raptiva (Efalizumab)?

Raptiva, developed by Genentech and marketed in Europe by Merck Serono, was a **recombinant humanized monoclonal antibody** approved for the treatment of moderate-to-severe chronic plaque psoriasis in adults. It received FDA approval in 2003 and EMA authorization in 2004.

The drug worked by targeting a specific immune pathway. Efalizumab bound to the CD11a subunit of lymphocyte function-associated antigen-1 (LFA-1), a protein found on the surface of T-cells. By blocking this molecule, the medication:

- Inhibited the activation of T-lymphocytes
- Prevented T-cells from migrating into skin tissue
- Reduced the inflammatory cascade responsible for psoriatic plaques

Administered as a weekly subcutaneous injection, Raptiva offered a convenient option for patients who had not responded adequately to, or could not tolerate, other systemic therapies. However, the same immunosuppressive mechanism that made it effective also created a dangerous vulnerability.

## The Connection to PML

### What Is Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy?

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is a rare, progressive, and often fatal demyelinating disease of the central nervous system. It is caused by reactivation of the **John Cunningham virus (JC virus)**, a common pathogen that lies dormant in the majority of the adult population without causing harm.

In healthy individuals, the immune system keeps the JC virus in check. However, in people with severely weakened immune systems—such as those undergoing prolonged immunosuppressive therapy—the virus can reactivate, attacking the myelin sheath that insulates nerve fibers in the brain. Symptoms of PML include:

- Progressive weakness on one side of the body
- Clumsiness and impaired coordination
- Vision disturbances
- Cognitive decline, confusion, and personality changes
- Difficulties with speech and language

PML has no known cure, and the disease frequently leads to severe disability or death within months of onset.

### Efalizumab and PML Cases

Because Raptiva suppressed T-cell function on a chronic basis, it compromised the immune surveillance that normally prevents JC virus reactivation. In late 2008 and early 2009, reports emerged of patients who had been taking Raptiva for extended periods—generally more than three years—developing confirmed cases of PML.

At least **three confirmed cases and one suspected case** of PML were reported among patients using the drug, with several resulting in death. These patients had no other identifiable cause of immunosuppression, pointing strongly to efalizumab as the contributing factor. Given that psoriasis, while serious, is not a life-threatening condition, the emergence of a fatal brain infection dramatically altered the risk-benefit calculation for the medication.

## Regulatory Response: FDA and EMA Actions

### European Medicines Agency

The EMA acted first and most decisively. In February 2009, the agency's Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) reviewed the accumulating safety data and concluded that **the benefits of Raptiva no longer outweighed its risks**. The committee recommended the **suspension of the marketing authorization** across the European Union.

The EMA advised that:

- Doctors should **stop prescribing** Raptiva and begin transitioning patients to alternative treatments
- Patients should **not stop treatment abruptly** without consulting their physician, to avoid a rebound worsening of psoriasis
- Patients should be **monitored for neurological symptoms** both during treatment and for a period afterward

Merck Serono subsequently withdrew the drug from the European market.

### U.S. Food and Drug Administration

In the United States, the FDA issued a **public health advisory** and added a **boxed warning**—the agency's most serious warning—to the Raptiva label in October 2008, alerting healthcare providers and patients to the risk of life-threatening infections, including PML.

By April 2009, following additional PML reports, Genentech announced a **phased voluntary withdrawal** of Raptiva from the U.S. market in cooperation with the FDA. The agency emphasized that:

- New patients should **not be started** on the drug
- Current patients should **consult their healthcare providers** about transitioning to alternative therapies
- Abrupt discontinuation should be **medically supervised**
- Patients and providers should **remain vigilant** for signs of infection and neurological changes

The withdrawal was structured over several months to allow patients and physicians adequate time to arrange safe alternative treatments.

## Patient Safety Recommendations

The Raptiva warnings prompted a set of important safety recommendations that remain relevant to biologic therapy in general:

1. **Do not discontinue abruptly:** Patients were strongly urged to work with their physicians on a supervised transition plan, as suddenly stopping the medication could trigger a severe rebound flare of psoriasis.

2. **Monitor for neurological symptoms:** Any new or worsening symptoms—such as progressive weakness, coordination problems, vision changes, or cognitive difficulties—warranted immediate medical evaluation.

3. **Ongoing vigilance after cessation:** Because PML can develop even after the drug is stopped, former patients were advised to remain alert to symptoms for an extended period.

4. **Report adverse events:** Healthcare providers and patients were encouraged to report suspected side effects to regulatory bodies through pharmacovigilance channels such as the FDA's MedWatch program.

5. **Explore alternative therapies:** A range of other systemic treatments and biologics remained available, and physicians were advised to individualize treatment plans based on each patient's disease severity and risk profile.

## Broader Implications and Lessons Learned

The Raptiva case illustrates the complex trade-offs inherent in treating chronic, non-fatal conditions with powerful immunosuppressive agents. Several key lessons emerged:

- **Post-marketing surveillance is essential.** The PML cases came to light years after approval, underscoring the importance of long-term pharmacovigilance even after a drug reaches the market.

- **Risk-benefit assessments are dynamic.** A medication deemed acceptable at approval may be reevaluated as new safety data accumulate, particularly for conditions that are not life-threatening.

- **Immunosuppression carries inherent risks.** The connection between JC virus reactivation and immunomodulatory drugs has since informed the monitoring protocols for other biologics, including natalizumab (used in multiple sclerosis and Crohn's disease), which carries a similar PML risk.

- **Coordinated international action matters.** The parallel responses by the EMA and FDA demonstrated how regulatory agencies collaborate and act on shared safety concerns.

## Conclusion

The withdrawal of Raptiva (efalizumab) from the global market in 2009 marked a significant moment in dermatology and pharmacovigilance. While the drug offered genuine relief to many psoriasis patients, its association with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy—a devastating and often fatal brain infection—proved unacceptable given the nature of the condition it treated. The coordinated warnings and market withdrawals by the FDA and EMA reflected a commitment to patient safety over commercial or therapeutic convenience.

For patients living with psoriasis today, the Raptiva story is a reminder of both the promise and the peril of advanced biologic therapies. Fortunately, the field has continued to evolve, and a new generation of targeted treatments now offers effective options with more favorable safety profiles. As always, patients are encouraged to work closely with their healthcare providers to weigh the benefits and risks of any treatment and to remain informed participants in their own care.

---

*This article is intended for informational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice. Patients with questions about psoriasis treatments should consult a qualified healthcare professional.*

# Raptiva: How a Psoriasis Treatment's Immune Suppression Led to Fatal Brain Infections

## A Cautionary Tale in Immunosuppressive Therapy

Psoriasis affects an estimated **7.5 million Americans**, according to the National Psoriasis Foundation, making it one of the most common autoimmune conditions in the United States. For patients with moderate to severe forms of the disease, the search for effective treatments has sometimes led down dangerous paths—as the story of Raptiva demonstrates.

## What Was Raptiva?

Raptiva (efalizumab), manufactured by Genentech, received FDA approval in 2003 as a biologic treatment for chronic moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. The drug was a monoclonal antibody administered by weekly injection.

## The Mechanism: How Immune Suppression Creates Risk

Raptiva worked by targeting a protein called CD11a, found on the surface of T-cells—key players in the immune system. By binding to this protein, the drug prevented T-cells from:

- **Activating** in response to threats
- **Migrating** into the skin, where they drive psoriasis inflammation
- **Functioning** in normal immune surveillance

While this action successfully reduced psoriasis symptoms, it came with an inherent problem: **the same immune cells that cause psoriasis also protect the body against infections.** By suppressing T-cell activity broadly, Raptiva compromised patients' ability to fight off pathogens—including dormant viruses that a healthy immune system normally keeps in check.

## The PML Threat

The most serious consequence was **progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)**, a rare but devastating brain infection.

PML is caused by the **JC virus**, which lies dormant in the majority of adults without causing harm. In immunocompromised individuals, however, the virus can reactivate and attack the brain's white matter, destroying the myelin that insulates nerve cells.

**PML mortality statistics are stark:**
- The condition kills approximately **30–50% of those who develop it**
- Survivors often suffer **severe, permanent neurological damage**, including cognitive decline, paralysis, and vision loss
- There is **no effective cure**; treatment focuses primarily on restoring immune function

## The Withdrawal

By 2009, the FDA had confirmed **multiple cases of PML** among Raptiva patients, including several deaths. Given that psoriasis is not life-threatening and safer alternatives existed, regulators determined the risks outweighed the benefits.

- **February 2009:** The FDA issued a black box warning and announced a phased withdrawal
- **April 2009:** Genentech voluntarily pulled Raptiva from the U.S. market
- The **European Medicines Agency** took similar action, suspending the drug's marketing authorization

## Lessons for Modern Medicine

The Raptiva case illustrates a fundamental tension in immunosuppressive therapy: **drugs powerful enough to quiet an overactive immune system may also disable the body's essential defenses.**

This episode influenced how regulators evaluate biologics today, reinforcing the importance of:
- Post-market surveillance
- Careful risk-benefit analysis for non-fatal conditions
- Patient monitoring for opportunistic infections

For the millions of Americans living with psoriasis, the withdrawal of Raptiva represented both a setback and a safeguard—a reminder that treatment innovation must always be weighed against patient safety.
